## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials yet. The starting network scored 0.000 dev success on both seeds, and we have no training-success figures, so we can't yet tell whether learning failed or generalisation failed. Two likely bottlenecks:
1. **Samples.** Four PPO epochs at the fixed compute budget allow only about 131k steps.
2. **Discounting.** gamma 0.95 shrinks the +1 exact-build bonus by about half over a 16-step episode, which weakens the signal for finishing exactly and calling DONE at the right time.

On the architecture side, the starting net sees only a 5×5 area and has no global context in its per-cell features. Layer ordering (fill lower missing cells anywhere first) may need whole-board information.

Round 1 follows the program's split so each effect can be attributed:
- (a) recipe-only: 2 PPO epochs (about 1.9× the samples), gamma 0.98, lambda 0.95;
- (b) architecture-only: deeper 2D network with pooled global context added back to every cell, and small-init output layers;
- (c) both together.

Until dev success rises above 0, I will rank by mean training success.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials ended with 0 dev success and 0 training success over the last 10% of training. They used the default recipe, a more-samples recipe and a global-context net, and none of them learned to build exactly. So the problem is learning itself, not generalisation. Every run finished in 63–83 s, far under the 900 s limit, so the compute budget limits training, not time. With 2–4 PPO epochs, the agent sees only about 100–230k steps, roughly 5–12k episodes, across an action space of about 257 actions. The cheapest way to get more samples is 1 PPO epoch: about 409k steps on the starting net, nearly double r1c1's 229k. With entropy at 0.01, the sampled policy may also stay too random to string together 6–16 correct placements. Round 2 therefore tests three things: 1 epoch for more samples, lower entropy for a sharper policy, and a footprint-convolution head with a wider per-column stem. All three use the same base recipe, so their results can be compared directly.

### Round 3
All 6 trials score 0 on both dev and training success. That includes the start net, recipe changes (1–2 PPO epochs, up to 405k steps, two entropy settings, gamma 0.95–0.98) and two equivariant architecture changes. Since nothing learns at all, the cause is probably not sample count or capacity. I have two hypotheses. (1) The world may not line up actions with observations the way it is described. If action indices map to cells with a transpose, flip or offset, the translation-equivariant heads used so far cannot learn the mapping. (2) The policy may collapse onto a poor local optimum, such as pressing DONE early because random placements earn negative reward. Round 3 tests both. Two heads can learn any mapping between positions: a learned remap of positions and a transformer with absolute position embeddings. The third candidate is an anti-collapse recipe on the start net. Any training success above 0 is informative, because dev success stays at 0 until builds are exact.

### Round 4
All nine trials scored exactly 0 training success and 0 dev success. That covers 1, 2 and 4 PPO epochs, 102k to 426k steps, gamma 0.9 to 0.98, entropy 0.002 to 0.03, and convolutional, global-context, footprint-conv and transformer networks. With the shaped per-cell reward, a normal world should give some exact training builds after 400k samples, so this pattern points to a world mismatch rather than slow learning. The most likely mismatch is in how action indices map to cells or brick types (transposed, type-minor ordering, a different anchor). Every head so far assumed the stated layout through translation-equivariant per-cell logits. The one remap attempt (r3c1) still sent its output through that equivariant head. This last round therefore tests layout-agnostic action heads: a flat linear head added to the starting network, a pure MLP policy, and learned action queries attending over cells. Each costs about the starting network's compute or less, which keeps sample counts high.
